section.title: The Valley of Vision
section.sectionRationale: Uniquely among the oracles against the nations, chapters 13 to 23, this burden falls not on a foreign power but on Jerusalem herself, called here the Valley of Vision. It exposes a city that parties instead of repenting, frantically shores up her defenses without looking to the God who made them, and ends with a pointed word to two individual officials, proud Shebna cast down and faithful Eliakim raised up.
section.thesis: Jerusalem, given every reason to weep and repent, instead feasts and boasts in her own defenses, ignoring the LORD who alone planned them long ago, while the LORD's word to two officials, Shebna deposed and Eliakim exalted, shows that even the most secure human position can be given and taken away.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the burden against the Valley of Vision and the prophet's refused comfort; Judah's frantic, self-reliant defenses; the fall of proud Shebna; and Eliakim raised up with the key of David, itself later shown to fail.

units.label: The burden against the Valley of Vision

verses.text: This is the burden against the Valley of Vision: What ails you now, that you have all gone up to the rooftops,
O city of commotion, O town of revelry? Your slain did not die by the sword, nor were they killed in battle.
All your rulers have fled together, captured without a bow. All your fugitives were captured together, having fled to a distant place.
Therefore I said, “Turn away from me, let me weep bitterly! Do not try to console me over the destruction of the daughter of my people.”
For the Lord GOD of Hosts has set a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the Valley of Vision, of breaking down the walls and crying to the mountains.

units.label: Frantic defenses, but not looking to the Maker

verses.text: Elam takes up a quiver, with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovers the shield.
Your choicest valleys are full of chariots, and horsemen are posted at the gates.
He has uncovered the defenses of Judah. On that day you looked to the weapons in the House of the Forest.
You saw that there were many breaches in the walls of the City of David. You collected water from the lower pool.
You counted the houses of Jerusalem and tore them down to strengthen the wall.
You built a reservoir between the walls for the waters of the ancient pool, but you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago.
On that day the Lord GOD of Hosts called for weeping and wailing, for shaven heads and the wearing of sackcloth.
But look, there is joy and gladness, butchering of cattle and slaughtering of sheep, eating of meat and drinking of wine: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!”
The LORD of Hosts has revealed in my hearing: “Until your dying day, this sin of yours will never be atoned for,” says the Lord GOD of Hosts.

units.label: The fall of proud Shebna
units.note: a self-made tomb, a coming shame

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says: “Go, say to Shebna, the steward in charge of the palace:
What are you doing here, and who authorized you to carve out a tomb for yourself here, to chisel your tomb in the height and cut your resting place in the rock?
Look, O mighty man! The LORD is about to shake you violently. He will take hold of you,
roll you into a ball, and sling you into a wide land. There you will die, and there your glorious chariots will remain, a disgrace to the house of your master.
I will remove you from office, and you will be ousted from your position.

units.label: Eliakim given the key of David
units.note: raised up, yet the peg itself will give way

verses.text: On that day I will summon My servant, Eliakim son of Hilkiah.
I will clothe him with your robe and tie your sash around him. I will put your authority in his hand, and he will be a father to the dwellers of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah.
I will place on his shoulder the {{mephtach|key}} to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open.
I will drive him like a {{yathad|peg}} into a firm place, and he will be a throne of glory for the house of his father.
So they will hang on him the whole burden of his father's house: the descendants and the offshoots, all the lesser vessels, from bowls to every kind of jar.
In that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, the peg driven into a firm place will give way; it will be sheared off and fall, and the load upon it will be cut down.” Indeed, the LORD has spoken.

mephtach.gloss: A key, an instrument of authority to open and shut, granted here to Eliakim over the house of David. The New Testament applies this exact image to Christ, who holds the key of David and controls all access to God's kingdom, Revelation 3:7.

yathad.gloss: A peg or tent stake driven into a wall to bear the weight of hanging vessels. Eliakim is driven in like a firm, load-bearing peg, yet the chapter's sober ending shows that even this peg will eventually give way, a reminder that human office, however faithfully held, cannot bear ultimate weight forever.

basic.context: Unlike its neighboring oracles against foreign nations, this burden falls on Jerusalem itself, called the Valley of Vision because she has received God's revelation yet fails to heed it. Facing a real military crisis, the city responds not with repentance but with frantic engineering projects and reckless partying, while the LORD singles out two officials by name, proud Shebna, who is deposed, and faithful Eliakim, who is exalted with remarkable authority.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a historical oracle, most plausibly tied to the Assyrian crisis under Sennacherib around 701 BC, when Jerusalem did in fact fortify her walls and water supply, recorded in 2 Kings 20:20 and 2 Chronicles 32. It describes a real failure of faith amid real engineering competence; the passage does not condemn practical preparation itself but the fatal substitution of self-reliant competence for trust in the LORD who planned these very resources long ago.
basic.originalLanguages: Eliakim is given the mephtach, the key, of the house of David, an image of total administrative authority that the New Testament applies directly to Christ, Revelation 3:7. He is also driven in like a yathad, a peg, bearing his father's household's whole weight, yet the oracle's sobering final word is that even this firm peg will one day give way.
basic.typology: Eliakim, clothed with robe and sash and given the key of David to open and shut with final authority, is an unmistakable type of Christ, who holds the key of David completely and whose authority, unlike Eliakim's, never gives way. The pattern of a faithful steward raised up after an unfaithful one is deposed anticipates the true and final steward of God's house.
basic.christ: Revelation 3:7 applies Eliakim's very words to Jesus, who holds the key of David, opening what no one can shut and shutting what no one can open. But where Eliakim, however faithful, is eventually described as a peg that will give way under its own household's weight, Christ is the true and final steward whose authority never fails and whose house never falls, Hebrews 3:6.
basic.god: God sees straight through frantic human competence to the heart's true trust, or lack of it; skillful engineering that ignores Him is no substitute for repentance. He is also sovereign over individual careers and offices, deposing the proud self-promoter Shebna and raising up the faithful Eliakim by His own initiative and timing.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 20:20 and 2 Chronicles 32:1-8 record Hezekiah's actual wall and water tunnel projects during this crisis. Revelation 3:7 applies Eliakim's key of David directly to Christ. Hebrews 3:1-6 contrasts Moses, a faithful servant in God's house, with Christ, the faithful Son over God's house, echoing this chapter's pattern of stewards who ultimately point beyond themselves.
basic.oneStory: Jerusalem's frantic self-reliance without repentance, and the rise and eventual limits of even a faithful steward like Eliakim, show that no human competence or office, however impressive, can finally secure God's house. Only Christ, who holds the key of David without limit, is the steward who never gives way.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a ring and a pair. The ring runs through verses 1 to 14. The city is first seen at play on its rooftops, verses 1 and 2, then the prophet breaks down in grief, verse 4, then the enemy arrives and the city busies itself with defenses, verses 6 to 11, then the LORD calls for grief, verse 12, and the city answers with a party, verse 13. Revelry opens the unit and revelry closes it, and weeping stands on either side of the middle. Isaiah weeps because the city will not, and the God who calls for weeping is answered with wine and meat.

The middle section is carried by a string of verbs addressed to the city. You looked, you saw, you collected, you counted, you tore down, you built, verses 8 to 11. Every one is an action of careful, even admirable, management. The whole list is then overturned by one clause. The city 'looked to the weapons' in verse 8 and 'did not look to the One who made it' in verse 11. The two looks are set deliberately at the two ends of the paragraph, so the reader sees how much the city saw and what it failed to see.

The second half of the chapter, verses 15 to 25, turns from a city to two men and from 'you' to a single speaker. The verbs now belong to God: I will remove you, I will summon, I will clothe, I will put, I will place, I will drive, verses 19 to 23. The phrase 'on that day' marks the hinges, verses 5, 8, 12, 20 and 25, and the last occurrence, in verse 25, reaches back to undo the confidence of verses 22 to 24.

The heading, 'the burden,' also frames the chapter. It opens in verse 1 and returns, at the very end, in the load that falls in verse 25.
context.historical:
The best fit for verses 8 to 11 is the summer and autumn of 701 BC. Sennacherib had taken the fortified cities of Judah, Isaiah 36:1, and was pressing Jerusalem. Hezekiah did what a competent king would do. He consulted his officers and stopped the springs outside the city, rebuilt breached sections of the wall, raised towers, added an outer wall and made weapons and shields in abundance, 2 Chronicles 32:3-5, and he channeled the water of Gihon down into the city, 2 Chronicles 32:30 and 2 Kings 20:20. A tunnel cut through the rock under the City of David, with an inscription at its lower end that records the two teams of diggers meeting, still carries that water. The 'House of the Forest' of verse 8 is Solomon's cedar building, where he stored hundreds of golden shields, 1 Kings 7:2 and 10:16-17, and it serves here as the city's armory.

The officers named in the oracle appear in the historical record. Eliakim son of Hilkiah is 'in charge of the palace' when the Assyrian spokesman arrives, with Shebna as the scribe and Joah as the recorder, 2 Kings 18:18 and Isaiah 36:3. Isaiah 37:2 shows Eliakim and Shebna, now with sackcloth, sent to Isaiah. Shebna's name appears as scribe, not steward, which fits the demotion announced in verse 19. A rock-cut tomb with an inscription for a royal steward was found near the village of Silwan, across the Kidron valley, and some scholars have linked it to Shebna, though the attribution is disputed.

Burial customs sharpen the oracle. Israelites wanted to be buried with their own people, Genesis 23:4, and dying 'on pagan soil' was a curse, Amos 7:17. The title 'in charge of the palace' also has a long history, from Joseph over Pharaoh's house, Genesis 41:40, to Ahishar under Solomon, 1 Kings 4:6. A man in that office held the king's confidence, and its key was a sign of delegated power.
context.canonical:
The oracle belongs to a family of passages where Jerusalem is the place that sees and does not see. The book opens with 'the vision of Isaiah,' Isaiah 1:1, and in chapter 29 the city called Ariel will find that 'the entire vision' is like words in a sealed scroll, Isaiah 29:11, because the LORD has poured out 'a spirit of deep sleep,' Isaiah 29:10. The Valley of Vision, then, is a city with a prophet's word in its streets and closed eyes in its heart.

The water-works recall an older scene at the same place. Isaiah met Ahaz at the end of the aqueduct of the upper pool and told him to be calm and unafraid, Isaiah 7:3-4, adding, 'If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all,' Isaiah 7:9. A generation later the water had been tamed, but trust had not been learned. The gently flowing waters of Shiloah had been rejected before, Isaiah 8:6. The story of Hezekiah, Isaiah 36 to 39, shows the same man able to trust gloriously in chapter 37 and to show the Babylonian envoys everything in chapter 39.

The New Testament quotes the slogan of verse 13 as the logic of a world without resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:32, and Jesus' parable of the rich fool is a little commentary on it, Luke 12:19-20. The key of verse 22 is cited by the risen Lord in His letter to Philadelphia, Revelation 3:7, and He is the one who holds 'the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:18. Hebrews sets Christ over the house as a Son, where Moses was a servant in it, Hebrews 3:5-6, and the image of a peg or stake from Judah is picked up in Zechariah 10:4 and in the promise that Zion's tent pegs will never be pulled up, Isaiah 33:20.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah's first hearers expected judgment to fall on Babylon, Philistia and Moab. This chapter turns the pointing finger back to the one place they thought they were safe. The prophet's intention is to expose a gap between what Jerusalem knew and how it lived. The city was called the Valley of Vision because it had prophets, the temple and a king who had seen deliverance. Yet when pressure came, it measured walls and water and was silent about God. What shocks Isaiah is not panic, which would at least be honest, but a celebration over sin.

The second half is meant to shake a different false security. Shebna had secured a high place, a chariot and a grave, and Judah's confidence had risen with him. By naming him, Isaiah teaches that even the highest offices in God's house are on loan. The promise of Eliakim is true comfort, and the last verse is a deliberate caution. Hearers are not to rest their weight on any human peg, however firmly set. The chapter prepares Judah to look beyond its officials to the LORD of Hosts who appoints and removes them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what a city did in a siege and what God did with two officials. It does not forbid defenses, water supplies or tombs, and it does not teach that every ambitious person will be deposed. Second Chronicles reports Hezekiah's works without blame, 2 Chronicles 32:30, and the fault named in verse 11 is that the city did not look to the One who planned the water long before. The slogan of verse 13, 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die,' is the city's own voice, quoted to expose it. Paul can cite it as the reasoning of unbelief, 1 Corinthians 15:32, but nowhere is it given as advice.

What carries over is the pattern. Believers are to ask what they are looking to when pressure comes, to weep when God calls for weeping, Joel 2:12-13, and to hold any position of authority as a trust from the One who gave it. Eliakim's promotion is a description of what God did for Judah in that hour, not a promise that God will install a particular official in every church or nation.

debates.question: Who is the peg in verse 25 that gives way?

views.label: Eliakim himself
views.case: Verse 25 repeats the words of verse 23, 'the peg driven into a firm place,' so the natural reader hears the same peg. Verse 24 has already told us what weighs on him: the whole family, from descendants to the smallest vessels, hangs on his office. The picture is of an honest man whose relatives overload him, and the sober point is that no human steward can bear that weight forever.

views.label: Shebna, in a flashback
views.case: Some take 'in that day' to refer back to the day Shebna is thrown out, so that the peg that gives way is the first officer, who also thought himself firmly placed. On this view the chapter ends with the confirmation of his fall.

views.label: A contrast that points beyond both officials
views.case: Others read verse 25 as the door left open for a greater steward. The word 'firm' in verse 23 has the sense of faithful and sure, and a faithful peg that finally yields shows that the ultimate key belongs to someone else, which Revelation 3:7 takes up.

debates.bearing: The grammar favours Eliakim, because the same description is used twice. The chapter's logic then moves from comfort to caution. Even the faithful man who is raised up is not the final source of the house's stability, and this prepares for the fuller fulfilment in Christ.

debates.question: Which crisis lies behind verses 1 to 14?

views.label: Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC
views.case: Verses 8 to 11 match Hezekiah's preparations point for point, and the officials in verse 15 are Hezekiah's men. The revelry of verse 13 would suit the city's reaction after Hezekiah paid tribute and the Assyrians withdrew for a time, 2 Kings 18:14-16, or after the later deliverance, Isaiah 37:36.

views.label: The fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC
views.case: The rulers who flee and are captured 'without a bow,' verse 3, remind some readers of Zedekiah and his army fleeing by night and being overtaken, 2 Kings 25:4-7. On this reading Isaiah sees the city's end and the preparations of 701 as its prelude.

views.label: A prophetic picture that blends crises
views.case: A third view holds that Isaiah's vision speaks to the city's habit, a pattern repeated on both occasions, and that precise dating matters less than the pattern of frantic effort without repentance.

debates.bearing: Most of the concrete detail points to 701, and verse 3 can be read as fugitives overtaken in the countryside. The oracle still speaks with force to any later generation that repeats the pattern.

debates.question: How does Revelation 3:7 use the key of David?

views.label: A direct application of Isaiah 22:22 to Christ
views.case: The wording is nearly identical, 'What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open.' John does not quote Isaiah by name, but he gives Jesus the same title, key of David, and the same sealed authority, so the passage is treated as pointing beyond Eliakim to the son of David who holds the key by right.

views.label: A borrowed image for a related claim
views.case: Other readers say Revelation takes the image of the steward's key and applies it to Christ's authority over the doors of the church, Revelation 3:8, without claiming that Isaiah 22 was a prediction. The link is typological resonance, not fulfilled prophecy.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that Christ holds the authority Eliakim only held on loan, and Revelation 1:18 shows how far it goes, to the keys of Death and of Hades.

study.originalLanguages:
The name of the city, 'the Valley of Vision,' is built on the root for seeing a vision, the same root that gives the noun for vision in the opening line of the book, Isaiah 1:1. Jerusalem is the place where prophecy is seen. The irony of verse 11 depends on that. The city is named for vision and cannot see the One who made its pool.

Verse 11 uses two verbs of the Creator that appear together elsewhere. The One who 'made' it and who 'planned' it long ago use the verbs for making and for forming, the second of which is the potter's word. The phrase 'long ago' is literally 'from afar.' The same pair appears in Isaiah 37:26, where the LORD tells Sennacherib that 'long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it.' The water of Jerusalem and the rise of Assyria are both works of a God who plans from far off, which is why neither a pool nor a siege takes Him by surprise.

Verse 14 says the sin 'will never be atoned for' until the people die. The verb is the one behind the word for atonement, the root of Yom Kippur. The sentence takes the form of an oath, an 'if' clause whose result is left unsaid, the same form used against the house of Eli in 1 Samuel 3:14. It means the sin is outside the reach of the usual sacrifices because it was committed with open contempt for a call from God, compare Numbers 15:30-31, where the person who sins 'defiantly' has despised the word of the LORD.

In verses 23 and 25 the 'firm place' comes from the root that gives the Hebrew for faith and for 'amen.' It is the root behind Isaiah 7:9, 'If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.' The word is also used for the sure house promised to David, 2 Samuel 7:16, and for the faithful mercies of David, Isaiah 55:3. Eliakim is set in a place of faithfulness, and the question is whether anyone can be that place for others.

The word glory is at work across verses 18 to 24. Shebna's 'glorious chariots,' verse 18, will be a disgrace, and Eliakim is made a 'throne of glory,' verse 23. In verse 24 the Hebrew behind the BSB's 'burden' is the word for glory, which also carries the sense of weight, so that the whole honor of the family hangs on him as a heavy load.

Finally, the oracle opens in verse 1 with the heading massa, the burden, and ends in verse 25 with a related noun, the load that is cut down. The word of judgment and the weight on the peg are one idea at the two ends of the chapter.

typology.type: The key of David and the doors that cannot be shut or opened, Isaiah 22:22
typology.fulfillment: Eliakim is given the key to the house of David and the authority to open and shut, but the authority is borrowed, since the house belongs to the king. The risen Christ takes the same words, Revelation 3:7, and He is Himself the son of David who will reign on David's throne forever, Luke 1:32-33. The government that rests on His shoulder, Isaiah 9:6-7, is the heavier burden of Isaiah 22:22, and He holds the keys not only of a house but of Death and of Hades, Revelation 1:18. The type falls short because Eliakim's key opens a household, while Christ's opens an open door for the church, Revelation 3:8, that no one can shut.

typology.type: The tomb hewn for oneself, Isaiah 22:16
typology.fulfillment: Shebna cut a resting place in the rock for his own glory and will die in a distant land, never using it. In the Gospels another rock-cut tomb appears, one 'that he had cut into the rock,' belonging to a rich man named Joseph, Matthew 27:60, which fits Isaiah's phrase that the Servant was 'with a rich man in His death,' Isaiah 53:9. Jesus was laid in a tomb that was not His own and left it empty. This is an echo, not a declared type, and it works by contrast: the self-made grave of the proud steward ends in disgrace, while the borrowed grave of the humble Son becomes the place of resurrection.

typology.type: The peg that bears the weight of the house, Isaiah 22:23-25
typology.fulfillment: A peg holds up a household's whole weight, and Eliakim is a faithful one who nonetheless gives way. The promise that a tent peg will come from Judah, Zechariah 10:4, and that the cornerstone laid in Zion will never be shaken, Isaiah 28:16, finds its answer in Christ, 'the cornerstone,' Ephesians 2:20, in whom 'all things hold together,' Colossians 1:17, and who upholds all things by His powerful word, Hebrews 1:3. He invites the weary and burdened to come to Him, Matthew 11:28, and does not buckle under what hangs on Him. The type fails by design, so that the reader looks beyond it.

typology.type: The city that will not weep, Isaiah 22:12-13
typology.fulfillment: The LORD calls for weeping and the city feasts. The scene repeats when Jesus approached Jerusalem, saw it, and wept, saying that they had not recognized the time of their visitation, Luke 19:41-44, and when He lamented that He had longed to gather her children 'but you were unwilling,' Matthew 23:37-38. The prophet's refusal to be consoled, verse 4, becomes the Messiah's tears. The correspondence is of a city in two generations missing its moment. The escalation is that the One who weeps is the God who sent the warning.

study.christ:
The clearest line from this chapter to Christ is the one the New Testament draws itself. In the letter to Philadelphia, the risen Lord introduces Himself as 'the One who is holy and true, who holds the key of David. What He opens no one can shut, and what He shuts no one can open,' Revelation 3:7. John did not coin that language. It is Isaiah's description of Eliakim, now spoken by the One for whom Eliakim was a preparation. The correspondence is rich. Eliakim is called 'My servant,' verse 20, a title the book later gives to the Servant who will prosper and be lifted up, Isaiah 52:13. He is a father to Jerusalem, verse 21, and the Son who comes is called Everlasting Father, Isaiah 9:6. The government is on his shoulder, verse 22, as the government is on the shoulders of the promised child, Isaiah 9:6-7. And Eliakim's throne of glory, verse 23, becomes the throne of David that Mary is told her Son will receive, Luke 1:32-33.

Then comes the contrast that makes the link honest. Eliakim is a faithful steward in another man's house, appointed and finally removed, and the weight of his relatives breaks the peg, verse 25. Christ is not a steward in the house of David. He is David's son and David's Lord, and Hebrews says He is faithful 'as the Son over God's house,' not as a servant within it, Hebrews 3:5-6. He lives forever, so His office is permanent, Hebrews 7:24-25, and He holds keys no human steward could ever hold, 'the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:18.

The chapter also meets Christ at its two darkest verses. Paul quotes verse 13, 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die,' as the reasoning of people who deny the resurrection, and answers it with 'But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead,' 1 Corinthians 15:20 and 15:32. Verse 14 declares that this sin will not be atoned for until death, and Hebrews declares that Christ has appeared once for all 'to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself,' Hebrews 9:26. That does not cancel the warning of verse 14, because the city refused the very word that offered repentance. It shows where the answer to such a verse lies. And Jesus' tears over a city that did not recognize its visitation, Luke 19:41-44, are the tears Isaiah shed in verse 4 and the God who had asked the city to weep.

The link rests on what the New Testament states. Shebna's tomb, the pool and the shields are not coded pictures of Jesus.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that He sees what a city is looking at. Jerusalem collects water, counts houses and tears down some to shore up a wall, and every one of those actions is visible to Him. The verdict is not that the work was wrong but that the city 'did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago,' verse 11. God is the long-range planner. The spring in the city and the tunnel that brought it in were His provision before the siege, and the verb of making and forming used in verse 11 is the one He uses of Assyria's own rise in Isaiah 37:26. Nothing in the crisis is a surprise to Him, and the king's best work is already inside His plan.

He is a God who asks for the right response. The call of verse 12 is explicit: weeping, wailing, shaven heads and sackcloth. It is the appeal Joel will later make, 'return to Me with all your heart,' Joel 2:12. The LORD is not asking for display. He is asking for the kind of grief that turns a city toward Him. He is, in the same breath, the God who announces that deliberate contempt is outside the usual reach of sacrifice, verse 14. Holiness here is serious: the same God who cares for the city's water cannot be mocked by its feasting.

He is the Lord of offices. In the second half He speaks in the first person, 'I will remove you,' 'I will summon My servant,' 'I will clothe him,' 'I will place on his shoulder,' verses 19 to 22, and the earlier question to Shebna, 'who authorized you,' verse 16, shows that every post in Judah is His to grant. The long title, 'the Lord GOD of Hosts,' stands in verses 5, 12, 14 and 15, and it is used most often where the city has forgotten who is in command.

He holds mercy and judgment together. For David's sake He will later defend this city, Isaiah 37:35, yet He does not wink at its feasting. He appoints a faithful man for the good of the people, yet makes plain that even this steward will not be the final support. For worship, the chapter says to look at the Maker before the walls, to weep when He calls, and to rest the weight of life on the One who does not give way.

crossReferences.note: The chronicler records Hezekiah stopping the springs, rebuilding the wall, raising towers and producing weapons. It is the factual background to verses 9 to 11 and shows that the city's preparations were real and not condemned in themselves.

Eliakim son of Hilkiah is in charge of the palace, with Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder, meeting the Assyrian spokesman. It places both men from this oracle in the same crisis and shows Shebna already in the lesser office of scribe.

Isaiah meets Ahaz at the end of the aqueduct of the upper pool, near the water works of Isaiah 22, and tells him to be calm. The prophet's earlier word at this very spot shows the city had been taught to trust before it learned to dig.

The saying 'If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all' uses the same root as the 'firm place' in which Eliakim's peg is driven. It turns the peg into a question about faith, and about who can truly be firm.

The LORD tells Sennacherib that He ordained and planned his conquests long ago. The same verbs and the same 'long ago' appear in Isaiah 22:11, so the God who planned the pool is also the God who planned the invasion that sent Judah to it.

The call to return with fasting, weeping and mourning, to rend hearts and not garments, is the call that Isaiah 22:12 echoes. Joel also supplies what the city missed, that the LORD is gracious and compassionate and relents from sending disaster.

The oath that the iniquity of Eli's house 'shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering' shares its form with Isaiah 22:14. Both describe a point where repeated contempt places a sin beyond ordinary remedy.

Paul quotes 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' as the conclusion of a world with no resurrection. Isaiah's feasting city is the picture of that logic, and Paul's next words, that Christ is raised, give the answer.
The rich fool tells himself to 'Eat, drink, and be merry' and is told that his life will be required that night. Jesus' parable is a small commentary on the party of Isaiah 22:13.

Pharaoh puts Joseph in charge of his house and tells him that only the throne is greater. The office Eliakim receives has this kind of pedigree: a trusted servant with the king's authority over the household and the people.
The risen Christ says that He holds the key of David and that what He opens no one can shut. It takes the words of Isaiah 22:22 and attaches them to the One for whom Eliakim was a preparation.
Christ holds the keys of Death and of Hades. It shows how far the key of David extends in Him. Eliakim's key governed a palace, while this key governs the end of every life.

The government rests on the shoulders of the promised child, who reigns on David's throne. Isaiah 22:22 puts a key on a steward's shoulder; Isaiah 9 puts the whole government on a king's. The two passages speak to the same house.

Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, but Christ is faithful as the Son over it. The contrast is the same as that between Eliakim and Christ, a faithful steward set against the Son who owns the house.

study.oneStory:
Genesis begins with a world where humans are to look to God and live. By Genesis 3 they look at a tree and at each other, and the story from there is a long record of people who look at their resources and not at their Maker. Isaiah 22 is a late and vivid example. A city rich in prophecy, with a pool and a wall and a king, has every tool for life and refuses the one thing that makes the others work. 'Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain,' Psalm 127:1. The chapter is the Bible's picture of capable people with closed eyes.

The second movement shows the same story in a household. Joseph was lifted from a pit to stand over Pharaoh's house, Genesis 41:40, a servant who bore the king's authority for the sake of the people. Eliakim is raised in his place in Jerusalem, and Shebna is the opposite figure, the steward who used the office to make a name for himself. Every generation of Israel's leaders is a mixture of the two, and the nation's history, from Saul to the last kings, shows how even faithful pegs give way.

The story needs a peg that holds. Isaiah moves toward it in the child on whose shoulders the government rests, Isaiah 9:6-7, and the Servant who is lifted up, Isaiah 52:13. It arrives in the Son of David who holds the key, Revelation 3:7, who weeps over the city that did not know the time of its visitation, Luke 19:41-44, and who is raised so that 'tomorrow we die' is no longer the last word, 1 Corinthians 15:20. The house He keeps is not a palace in Jerusalem but a people, and Hebrews says 'we are His house,' Hebrews 3:6.

The new creation fulfils what the chapter lacked. There is a city with open gates, Isaiah 60:11, where the Lamb is the lamp, Revelation 21:23, and where the people who were once 'burdened' find rest, Matthew 11:28. No one hangs a household's weight on a human peg there, because the One who holds everything together, Colossians 1:17, dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. The Valley of Vision becomes the city where every eye finally sees.

quiz.q: How does Jerusalem respond to the crisis described in verses 1 to 5, instead of weeping and repenting?

options.text: With revelry and commotion, going up to the rooftops in a kind of frantic celebration.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2 describe exactly this response, commotion and revelry, not repentance.

options.text: With immediate, humble repentance and fasting.
options.note: The opposite; the prophet is asked to weep because the people are not weeping.

options.text: With total silence and withdrawal from public life.
options.note: Not what is described; the city is noisy with commotion and revelry, not silent.

options.text: With an organized evacuation of the entire city.
options.note: Some rulers flee, verse 3, but the city's overall posture described is revelry, not orderly evacuation.

quiz.q: What is the LORD's specific complaint about Jerusalem's defensive preparations, verses 9 to 11?

options.text: They fortified walls and secured water but did not look to the One who planned it all long ago.
options.note: Verse 11 states this precisely: competent preparation without trust in God.

options.text: They refused to build any defenses at all.
options.note: The opposite; they built extensive, competent defenses, which is not itself condemned.

options.text: They built defenses using forbidden foreign materials.
options.note: Not the stated complaint; the issue is the heart behind the preparation, not the materials.

options.text: They spent too much money on the temple instead of the walls.
options.note: Not addressed in this text; the complaint concerns trust, not budget allocation between temple and walls.

quiz.q: What happens to Shebna, the palace steward, according to this oracle?

options.text: He is deposed and cast far away, disgraced despite building himself a grand tomb.
options.note: Verses 15 to 19 describe his removal from office and disgrace in a distant land.

options.text: He is promoted to an even higher office.
options.note: The opposite; he is removed from office, not promoted.

options.text: He successfully defends his position against the prophet's rebuke.
options.note: No such defense is recorded; the oracle simply pronounces his removal.

options.text: He repents and is restored to his former position.
options.note: No repentance or restoration is mentioned in this passage; Eliakim replaces him instead.

quiz.q: What authority is Eliakim given, and how does the New Testament use this image?

options.text: The key of the house of David, later applied directly to Christ in Revelation 3:7.
options.note: Verse 22 gives Eliakim this key, and Revelation 3:7 applies the same image to Jesus.

options.text: Authority only over foreign nations, never over Jerusalem.
options.note: The opposite; his authority is specifically over the house of David and Jerusalem.

options.text: Authority to write new Scripture.
options.note: Not described in this passage; his role is administrative stewardship, not prophetic authorship.

options.text: Military command over Judah's entire army.
options.note: His role is described as a father and steward over the household and city, not specifically military command.

quiz.q: What sobering note does the chapter add about Eliakim's own position, verse 25?

options.text: Even the peg driven into a firm place will eventually give way and fall.
options.note: Verse 25 explicitly states that Eliakim's own secure position will eventually fail, pointing beyond him.

options.text: Eliakim's authority will last forever without any limit.
options.note: The opposite; the text specifically limits and eventually ends his tenure.

options.text: Eliakim will be immediately replaced by Shebna again.
options.note: Not stated in the text; no return of Shebna is mentioned.

options.text: Eliakim's family will be exempted from ever bearing responsibility.
options.note: The opposite; his household bears the whole burden, described in verse 24, until the peg gives way.

questions: Jerusalem was called to weep and repent but chose revelry instead, saying, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Where might you be avoiding hard truths with distraction or denial rather than honest repentance?
The city built impressive defenses but did not look to the One who planned them long ago. What competent, practical steps are you taking in life without pausing to actually trust God in the process?
Shebna built himself a grand tomb, seeking his own glory, and was brought low. Where are you tempted to build your own monument rather than serve faithfully in the place God has given you?

Eliakim was raised up as a faithful steward, yet even his firm position would eventually give way. What earthly role, relationship, or achievement are you resting your ultimate security on that cannot bear that weight forever?
Christ alone holds the key of David without limit, opening what no one can shut. How does resting in His unfailing authority free you from needing every human structure in your life to be permanent?

translationNotes.note: The Valley of Vision most likely refers to Jerusalem itself, ironically named for the revelation she has received yet fails to heed; some understand it as a specific valley within or near the city.
